subtype: Rejection from a placement or programme [Actor]
passage: Note by Vinita, placement officer. Tarun learned on Wednesday that the company he had prepared for over four months had not selected him. I found him at the back of the library, not studying. He said he felt embarrassed after telling everyone he would get it, jealous of two classmates who were selected, and doubtful about his ability. I did not offer a pep talk. I said the panel had picked eight from two hundred, and that fit, timing and the day's questions matter alongside merit. Tarun nodded slowly, not yet convinced. We agreed he would list what the interview taught him and come back on Friday. Follow-up scheduled. - Vinita

subtype: Rejection from a placement or programme [Actor]
passage:
In Amman, the email arrived at 11 p.m.: "We regret to inform you…" Nour had spent four months on that research programme application. Two recommendation letters, three drafts of the essay, an interview in which she'd thought she did well.
Across the room, her flatmate Ingrid was on the phone to her parents, laughing. She had got into the same programme an hour earlier.
Nour smiled, said "Congratulations," and meant it, mostly. Then she went into the bathroom and cried into a towel. She felt jealous and then ashamed of feeling jealous. Was she just not good enough?
In the morning she reread the email. It said there were 900 applicants for 25 places. Her professor, when she told him, said, "They took mostly people working on water. Your topic is soil. It's fit, Nour, not worth."
She didn't quite believe it yet. But she wrote it on a sticky note and put it on her mirror.

qa.q: How many applicants were there, and for how many places?
qa.a: There were 900 applicants for 25 places.

qa.q: How did Nour feel when Ingrid got into the programme?
qa.a: Nour felt jealous, then ashamed of the jealousy, and doubtful about being good enough.

qa.q: What could help Nour hold on to the professor's words?
qa.a: Keeping the note on her mirror and remembering the numbers and the topic fit, so she sees the rejection as about fit and competition.

qa.q: How might Ingrid feel if she knew Nour had cried?
qa.a: Ingrid might feel sad and a bit awkward, torn between her own joy and sympathy for her friend.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult rejected after long preparation who feels envy, embarrassment and doubt, while the rejection reflects fit and competition.

subtype: Rejection from a placement or programme [Actor]
passage:
In the college placement cell, the list went up on the noticeboard at three. Elizabeth scanned it twice. Her name wasn't there. Jasleen's was.
She had cleared three rounds with the firm: the test, the group discussion, the technical interview. She had prepared for two months. She had told her parents.
Jasleen found her in the corridor and hugged her, then stopped, seeing her face. "Oh, Liz."
"Congrats. Really," Elizabeth said, and walked quickly to the washroom. She hated that the first thing she felt was envy. The second was embarrassment. She had told everyone.
Later, the placement officer, Mrs Kuriakose, called her in. "They took four from two hundred. The final round was mostly about who could join in June. You said August for your project. That's timing, not ability."
Elizabeth nodded. It didn't feel like timing. It felt like being not enough. But she wrote down the names of two firms Mrs Kuriakose suggested.

qa.q: How many students did the firm take, and from how many?
qa.a: They took four from two hundred.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth feel first and second after seeing the list?
qa.a: First envy, then embarrassment, because she had told everyone.

qa.q: What small step does Elizabeth take at the end, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She writes down two firms Mrs Kuriakose suggested, a concrete next step even though the rejection still hurts.

qa.q: How does Jasleen seem to feel in the corridor?
qa.a: Jasleen is happy but stops when she sees Elizabeth's face, feeling sympathy and a little awkward.

grounding: Shows a young adult turned down after long preparation who feels envy and embarrassment, while the officer explains it was timing, not ability.

subtype: Rejection from a placement or programme [Actor]
passage:
Dear Gopika,
I didn't answer your calls this week, and I'm sorry. The design school sent their decision on Monday. It was a no.
I had spent a year on that portfolio. You know how many Sundays. When I read the email, I felt my face go hot, as if everyone could see it. Then I opened a photo app and saw a girl from my coaching class posting her acceptance, and I felt so jealous I had to put the phone in a drawer.
For three days I thought, maybe I'm not actually good at this.
Then my old teacher reminded me they took eighty students from six thousand, and that my work is illustration-heavy, while their course leans towards product design. Fit, she said, not talent.
I don't feel that yet. But I'm going to show my portfolio at the open day in Pune next month. Will you come with me?
Mahima

qa.q: How many students did the design school take, and from how many?
qa.a: They took eighty students from six thousand.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when the girl from coaching posted her acceptance?
qa.a: Mahima felt so jealous that the phone had to go in a drawer, and then doubted being good at design.

qa.q: What small next step has Mahima chosen?
qa.a: Showing the portfolio at the Pune open day next month, and asking Gopika to come along.

qa.a: Gopika might feel relieved to hear from Mahima, sympathetic about the rejection and glad to be asked to come along.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult rejected after long preparation who feels envy and self-doubt, while the rejection reflects fit and competition.

subtype: Rejection from a placement or programme [Actor]
passage:
Honestly, Yogesh, I wasn't going to talk about this, but fine. You got the design internship. I didn't. I prepared for four months: portfolio redone twice, mock interviews every Sunday. When the list came out and my name wasn't on it, I smiled, said congratulations to you, and then went and sat in the bike shed for an hour.
I'm Jeevan, and I'll admit it: I was jealous. Not of you exactly; of that email. Then embarrassed, because everyone in our hostel knew I'd applied. Then worse: I started thinking maybe I'm just not good enough and my teachers were only being kind.
Yesterday the placement officer told me they took only two people from four hundred applications, and both had worked on packaging projects like theirs. My portfolio is all furniture. That helped a little. It still stings. I'm applying to a furniture studio in Jaipur next week.

qa.q: How many people did the internship take, and from how many applications?
qa.a: They took only two people from four hundred applications.

qa.q: What did Jeevan feel when the list came out?
qa.a: Jeevan felt jealous of the email, then embarrassed because the hostel knew, and then doubtful about being good enough at all.

qa.q: What next step is Jeevan taking, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Applying to a furniture studio next week fits, since Jeevan's portfolio is all furniture and the rejection was partly about fit.

qa.q: What might it be like for Yogesh to hear this?
qa.a: Yogesh might feel awkward and sad, learning that the smile and congratulations hid an hour alone in the bike shed.

grounding: Shows a young adult turned down after long preparation feeling envy, embarrassment and doubt, before seeing the role of fit and competition.
